"I sincerely hope that my actions have not diminished the partnership that our two nations have developed together," the letter said. Hammond said the soldier's actions were tantamount to "criminal behavior." "I've come to this land to protect you, to support you -- not to harm you -- and the behavior of this soldier was nothing short of wrong and unacceptable," the general said. "I have asked that first this apology be officially documented; second a guarantee from the U.S. military to inflict the maximum possible punishment on this soldier so it would be a deterrent for the rest of the soldiers in the future." Bush has personally reached out to Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to offer his "deep regret" after a U.S. soldier used a copy of the Quran for target practice near Baghdad, an incident that has sparked intense outrage across Iraq and threatened fragile diplomatic relations.

White House Press Secretary Dana Perino confirmed Tuesday that President Bush brought up the incident during a pre-scheduled video conference with Maliki, making an explicit apology on behalf of the United States.

"The President expressed his deep regret to the Prime Minister," Perino told reporters. "He told him that we take this matter very seriously, and he apologized for the soldier's actions. He noted that the soldier has been disciplined and removed from Iraq."

According to a statement from the Iraqi Prime Minister’s office, Maliki accepted the apology but underscored the gravity of the incident, warning that such acts "offend the feelings of all Muslims and could damage the relationship between the two countries."

### Military Moves Quickly to Contain Fallout

The incident occurred on May 11 at a military firing range in Radwaniyah, a predominantly Sunni area west of Baghdad. An Iraqi police officer discovered a copy of the Islamic holy book riddled with bullet holes and inscribed with profanity on its pages. 

U.S. military officials identified the soldier involved as Staff Sgt. Joseph T. Morris, a sniper assigned to the 4th Infantry Division. Military officials immediately relieved the soldier of his duties, issued him a formal reprimand, and moved to transport him out of the country.

In an unprecedented public display of contrition, Maj. Gen. Jeffrey Hammond, commander of U.S. forces in Baghdad, traveled to Radwaniyah over the weekend to personally apologize to local tribal leaders and residents. 

Standing before an audience of Iraqi officials and elders, Hammond kissed a fresh copy of the Quran and formally presented it to the community leaders.

"I come before you seeking your forgiveness," Hammond said during the ceremony. "In the most humbled manner, I look at you and say: Please forgive me and my soldiers."

Commanders emphasized that the sniper’s actions were an isolated incident and counter to military values. "This was a despicable act, and it does not represent the thousands of men and women serving in Iraq who respect the religion and culture of the Iraqi people," said Rear Adm. Patrick Driscoll, a U.S. military spokesman in Baghdad.

### Furious Local Reaction

Despite the high-level apologies, the desecration has fueled deep resentment among Iraqis at a time when the U.S. military is attempting to solidify security gains made during the recent troop "surge."

In Radwaniyah, hundreds of local residents and members of the "Sons of Iraq"—the U.S.-backed Sunni militia groups crucial to reducing violence in the region—gathered to protest the act. Protesters burned American flags and held banners reading, "No, no to America" and "Insulting the Quran is an insult to all Muslims."

"We are standing alongside the Americans to fight al Qaeda, but this is how they repay us? By shooting our holy book?" said Sheikh Ahmed al-Ghreib, a local Sunni tribal elder who attended the protest. "Apologies are not enough. We want this soldier brought to justice under Iraqi law."

The backlash spread to Baghdad’s parliament, where several lawmakers denounced the incident and demanded that the soldier face a formal trial rather than just administrative discharge. 

"This is not just a mistake; it is an attack on the faith of over a billion people," said Hajim al-Hassan, a prominent Sunni lawmaker. "If the U.S. wants to build trust, there must be real accountability."

### Strategic Stakes

The controversy comes at a delicate moment for Washington and Baghdad, as negotiators attempt to finalize a formal Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) that will dictate the legal framework for American troops remaining in Iraq beyond 2008. 

The issue of legal immunity for U.S. soldiers—a key sticking point in the talks—has been made even more contentious by the incident, with several Iraqi factions using the Quran desecration to argue against granting U.S. troops protection from local laws.

U.S. officials remain hopeful that the swift disciplinary action taken by the military, combined with President Bush's direct intervention, will prevent the anger from escalating into widespread violence or derailing ongoing diplomatic negotiations.

***

# U.S. Military Issues High-Level Apologies After Soldier Uses Quran for Target Practice in Iraq

**BAGHDAD — May 2008** — Senior U.S. military commanders in Iraq engaged in rapid damage control, delivering formal public apologies to Iraqi officials and Sunni tribal elders after an American soldier used a copy of the Quran for target practice. 

The incident, which occurred at a small arms firing range near Baghdad, raised fears of a widespread backlash at a delicate moment in the Iraq War, threatening the fragile security alliances the U.S. military had spent months building with local Sunni leaders.

---

### The Incident

On May 11, 2008, Iraqi security forces discovered a heavily damaged, bullet-ridden copy of the Quran at a military shooting range in Radhwaniya, a predominantly Sunni area southwest of Baghdad. 

Upon inspection, the holy book was found to contain 14 bullet holes. In addition to the bullet marks, profanities and anti-Islamic graffiti were written inside the pages and on the cover, and a target had been drawn on the text. 

A military investigation quickly identified the responsible soldier as **Staff Sergeant Craig Miller**, a sniper assigned to the 4th Brigade Combat Team, 101st Airborne Division. 

---

### High-Level Damage Control and Apology

Recognizing that the desecration of Islam's holiest book could trigger severe violence and destroy military relationships across the country, U.S. commanders reacted swiftly.

On May 17, 2008, **Major General Jeffrey Hammond**, commander of U.S. forces in Baghdad and the 4th Infantry Division, personally traveled to Radhwaniya to attend a formal reconciliation ceremony with local tribal leaders, police chiefs, and government officials.

During the ceremony, Gen. Hammond offered a direct and solemn apology:

> *"I come before you seeking your forgiveness,"* Hammond told the gathered elders. *"In the most humble manner, I look at you and I ask for forgiveness from you and from your people. The actions of one soldier were nothing more than criminal behavior. I’m here to tell you that this soldier’s actions were wrong. It was unacceptable."*

During the event, a U.S. officer read a formal statement of apology from **Lieutenant General Lloyd Austin** (then the second-highest ranking U.S. commander in Iraq). To demonstrate respect, Gen. Hammond presented local elders with a new, pristine copy of the Quran, wrapped in green silk, and formally bowed as he presented it.

---

### Disciplinary Action

The military moved quickly to remove the soldier from the country to prevent him from becoming a focal point for retaliation. 

Staff Sergeant Miller was:
* Immediately relieved of his duties and removed from his unit.
* Formally reprimanded under Article 15 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ).
* Reduced in rank and ordered to forfeit pay.
* Redeployed out of Iraq back to his home base in the United States.

Military spokespeople emphasized that Miller’s actions violated military regulations and core values, describing his behavior as an isolated act that did not reflect the conduct of the broader U.S. military.

---

### Strategic and Political Context

The incident occurred during a highly sensitive phase of the war—the height of the "Troop Surge" and the expansion of the **Sunni Awakening (Sahwa)** movement, also known as the "Sons of Iraq." 

Under this strategy, the U.S. military paid and supported local Sunni tribesman and former insurgents who had turned against Al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI). This coalition was largely credited with drastically reducing violence across Anbar province and Baghdad.

Because the desecration occurred in a Sunni-dominated area heavily reliant on these tribal alliances, U.S. officials feared the act could cause Sunni fighters to turn their weapons back on American forces.

Local Iraqi response was marked by anger, but public protests were largely contained due to the swiftness and humility of the U.S. response. **Sheikh Aifan al-Eissawi**, a prominent Sunni Awakening leader in the region, accepted the apology on behalf of the local leadership but emphasized the severity of the act:

> *"This behavior was an insult not just to Iraqis, but to all Muslims,"* local leaders noted during the ceremony, while acknowledging that the military's prompt disciplinary action helped prevent an escalation into violent unrest.

---

### Aftermath

The U.S. military’s swift public intervention succeeded in preventing the event from escalating into nation-wide violent protests, which had occurred during previous incidents of religious desecration, such as the 2005 reports of Quran mistreatment at Guantanamo Bay. 

The 2008 Radhwaniya incident remains one of the most notable examples of top-level U.S. military commanders personally delivering a public, formal apology on foreign soil to preserve strategic political and military partnerships.
